food:
Clean cel-shaded anime game illustration of food with a touch of realism, like polished official item art in a Japanese action game: semi-realistic forms, proportions, lighting and materials; crisp, well-defined ink outlines of confident even weight around every object and every food piece, with clean hard edges and clear separation between pieces; large areas of smooth colour with two- or three-tone cel shading and a few soft gradients; sharp white gloss highlights; bright, appetising, slightly richer colours; plump juicy shapes; simple stylized steam curls. How to draw food surfaces: cooked egg is smooth, silky and glossy in large soft folds and sheets — never curdled, foamy, bubbly, crumbly or pebbly; simmering liquid is a smooth glossy surface with only a few small, clean bubbles near the edge — no foam, no dense bubbles; rice is a smooth soft mound with a few dozen individually outlined, same-size grains on the top and edges, never a noisy field of tiny grains; wood is smooth with a few long grain lines. All surfaces clean: no texture, no grain, no noise, no hatching or cross-hatching, no pencil, no stippling, no mosaic or crackle pattern, no paper texture. Tight close crop on the subject, three-quarter view from above. Minimal scenery: only the items the scene mentions, on a plain clean off-white background with a simple soft shadow. No text, no labels, no lettering, no watermark, no people, no animals or characters.

Rules: smooth, clean surfaces with crisp, well-defined outlines — no grain, noise, hatching, stippling, paper or crackle texture anywhere. Draw only what the scene names; nothing carried over from other steps. Food is in exactly the state the scene describes — nothing cooked, assembled or garnished ahead of time. Cooked egg is silky and glossy in soft folds, never curdled, foamy or pebbly; simmering liquid is smooth with only a few clean bubbles; rice is a soft mound with a modest number of clearly drawn grains. Cuts, sizes and quantities exactly as described and realistic. Any knife work uses a proper claw grip (guiding fingertips tucked under, knuckles against the blade). A chicken thigh fillet is small and thin — about palm-sized (12 × 8 cm), 1–2 cm thick, irregular, pale pink with a little white fat — never a big thick slab, never marbled red like pork or beef. Hands belong to one right-handed cook seen from their own position: the right hand does the knife/chopsticks/pouring work from the right side of the frame, the left hand steadies or holds the pan handle from the left; keep the camera angle the same across a recipe's pictures. Prefer a tight close-up where the subject fills the frame.

Scene: A cosy overhead spread on a smooth light-wood table: a dark lacquered donburi of oyakodon with silky egg, a white bowl of creamy ramen with spiral chashu slices, a soft egg and nori, a plate of tamagoyaki slices, a small dish of pink pickled red radish halves. Warm, appetising, minimal scenery.

How to draw small repeated things (rice grains, bubbles, crumbs, starch, flour, panko, crust nubs, sesame seeds, salt, sugar, chilli and spice flakes, bonito flakes, nori bits): draw each one INDIVIDUALLY as a distinct, separate piece — a simple clean shape with its own thin crisp outline, smooth cel shading and one small highlight, all at the same readable size (each at least about 1/80 of the picture width), like individually placed game sprites. Show a countable number — a few dozen, not hundreds. Never a dense swarm or speckled field, never clusters made of smaller clusters, never pieces shrinking into ever-tinier copies toward the edges: no fractal, self-similar, recursive, frothy, foamy, beaded, sponge-like or cauliflower-like surfaces. Where there would really be hundreds, draw the mass as one smooth flat-coloured shape and outline only a few dozen individual pieces on its surface and edges. Leave visible space between pieces — never a carpet of overlapping detailed pieces filling the frame. Small creatures (baby fish, tiny shrimp) are simplified to a clean silhouette with one eye dot — no scales, stripes or segments. Hot oil and simmering liquid: a smooth glossy surface with a dozen or so separate round bubbles, no froth. Fried crust is NOT made of pieces: a smooth, glossy, crisp shell following the food's softly lumpy shape, with a few soft creases and ridges and a handful of small flakes at its edges — never beads, dots, nubs, popcorn or cauliflower texture.
